title: Learning Python by Building Small Games
summary: Ping pong, Connect Four and tic-tac-toe in Tkinter: why tiny games were the fastest way for me to understand loops, state and events.
body: When I was still finding my feet as a developer, I noticed that tutorials taught me syntax but not how a program actually lives over time. So on a single day in May 2023 I pushed three small games to GitHub: Ping Pong, Connect Four and tic-tac-toe, all written with Python and Tkinter.
A game forces you to deal with the things that matter in every real application:

list: State: whose turn is it, what is on the board, what is the score.
Events: key presses and mouse clicks arrive whenever the user wants, not when your code is ready.
A loop: the screen has to be redrawn again and again without freezing the window.
Rules: checking four in a row in Connect Four is a nice exercise in working with 2D arrays.

body: For tic-tac-toe I built the same game twice, once in Tkinter and once in React. Writing identical logic in two worlds made it obvious which parts are the game (the board and the win check) and which parts are just the UI layer. That split between logic and presentation is something I still use every day.
If you are learning a new language, skip the tenth todo app and build a small game. You will run into real problems fast, and you will actually want to fix them.

title: Why My Portfolio Looks Like VS Code
summary: The idea behind this site: a Next.js portfolio with an explorer, tabs, themes and a title bar, built to feel like the editor I spend my days in.
body: I started this repository on 18 June 2023. I wanted a portfolio that says "developer" without a single word of text, and the most familiar screen in my life is VS Code. So the site is an editor: every page is a file, and you browse them with an explorer, a sidebar and tabs.

list: Next.js pages, each with getStaticProps, so every "file" is pre-rendered and fast.
A Zustand store, persisted to localStorage, that remembers which tabs you have open.
CSS variables for themes (Dracula, GitHub Dark, Ayu, Nord, Night Owl), switched by a data-theme attribute.
Small JSON files under /api for projects, experience and hobbies, so content lives apart from layout.

body.caption: The theme switcher: Dracula, GitHub Dark, Ayu, Nord and Night Owl.

body.h: The tabs were the hard part

body: Tabs look trivial until you implement them. Which tab should open when you close the active one? What happens when the saved tabs in localStorage do not match what the server rendered? I recently reworked this part so closing a tab behaves like VS Code: it focuses the tab to the right, or the left if there isn't one.
The project has been with me since 2023 and gets a new feature whenever I learn something worth showing. This blog is the newest file in the explorer.

cover.alt: Home page of this VS Code style portfolio

title: Coza Store: My First Full MERN Application
summary: Building an e-commerce store with MongoDB, Express, React and Node, and what splitting a project into client and server taught me.
body: Coza Store is an online shop I built with the MERN stack: MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js. It was the first project where I owned both sides: a React client and an Express server, living side by side in one repository.

The repo has exactly two top-level folders, client and server. That structure forced me to think about the API as a contract. The client should not care how products are stored, and the server should not care how they are displayed.

list: Designing REST endpoints for products, carts and users.
Modelling documents in MongoDB instead of tables.
Managing environment variables and CORS between two dev servers.
Deploying the frontend to Vercel.

body: I still come back to this project to try out new ideas, and it is one of the projects listed on this site.

title: A Summer Between Frontend and Backend
summary: Responsive pages with React and Mantine at Taskilled, and a Node.js CDN deployed on AWS with Docker and pm2 at Insightify.
body: The summer of 2023 was the busiest stretch of my career so far. In parallel with my full-stack role at TaskRider, I worked as a frontend developer at Taskilled and as a backend developer at Insightify. Switching between them every day taught me more than any course could.

My main job was responsive design. I built new pages with ReactJS and Mantine.dev and made sure existing ones worked on every screen size. Mantine's hooks and layout components saved a lot of time, but the real lesson was to design mobile-first and treat desktop as an enhancement.
On the backend side I built a CDN service with Node.js and Express, while the main backend ran on Next.js. I then deployed everything to AWS using Docker and kept the processes alive with pm2.

list: Docker made local and production environments identical.
pm2 gave me restarts, logs and zero-downtime reloads for free.
Serving static files well is mostly about caching headers.

body: Doing both sides at once made me a better developer on each. As a frontend developer I now think about payload size and caching. As a backend developer I think about what the UI actually needs.

title: What I Learned Building RPA Bots
summary: Automation Anywhere, IQ Bot document AI and co-pilot bots: notes from my time as an RPA developer at UpSystems.
body: From July 2023 to January 2024 I worked as an RPA developer at UpSystems LLC. Robotic Process Automation was a new world for me: instead of building apps for users, you build bots that use apps the way users do.

list: Automation bots in the Automation Anywhere Control Room.
Forms and processes that let people start and feed bots without technical knowledge.
Co-pilot bots that work alongside a human instead of replacing them.
Document AI with IQ Bot, extracting structured data from documents.

body: The biggest surprise was how much RPA is about the process, not the code. A bot is only as good as your understanding of the task it replaces, so most of the work is asking "what exactly happens when...?" before building anything.
It also gave me my first real experience with generative AI in production, which led straight into my next step: research on deep learning.

title: Deep Learning for Time Series Classification: My Reading List
summary: The papers I summarised during my research internship, from the UCR archive and FCN baselines to ROCKET, InceptionTime, LITE and attention.
body: In January 2024 I started a data science internship at the IRIMAS laboratory in France. My task was to read papers on time series classification (TSC), implement the models and compare results. To keep track of everything, I wrote a summary of each paper and published them as a small site: TSC_summaries.

list: The UCR Time Series Archive: the benchmark almost every paper reports on.
Time Series Classification from Scratch with Deep Neural Networks: A Strong Baseline (FCN, ResNet).
Deep learning for time series classification: a review.
ROCKET: exceptionally fast and accurate classification with random convolutional kernels.
InceptionTime: an ensemble of Inception-based networks.
LITE: a light Inception model with boosting tricks.
Disjoint-CNN for multivariate time series classification.
Enhancing TSC with self-supervised learning (TRILITE).
Attention Is All You Need, plus transformers for time series forecasting.

body: For every paper I wrote down four things: the problem, the core idea in one sentence, the architecture, and how it was evaluated. Then I implemented the model myself. In February 2024 I pushed my own versions of an MLP, logistic regression, ROCKET and InceptionTime. A paper only really made sense once the code ran.

body.alt: Positive sample generation with MixUp and masking
body.caption: From the TRILITE paper: a positive sample is made by mixing the reference with two other series, then masking part of it. Working through figures like this one was how I made sure I understood a method before implementing it.

body: If you are getting into TSC, start with the UCR archive paper and the FCN baseline, then read ROCKET. It will change what you think "deep" needs to mean.

cover.alt: Scatter plot of first-layer filters on the ArrowHead dataset

title: Five Months of Research at IRIMAS
summary: Reproducing LITE and TRILITE, building a custom Disjoint-CNN for multivariate time series, and learning how research actually works.
body: My internship at the IRIMAS laboratory in France ran from January to May 2024. It was my first time working full-time in a research lab instead of on products, and it changed how I approach problems.

The first rule I learned: before you try to beat a model, reproduce it. I re-implemented LITE, a lightweight Inception-style network for time series, and then worked with the code of TRILITE. TRILITE is a self-supervised approach that uses a triplet loss to learn representations from univariate UCR datasets, and it can also be trained semi-supervised.

body.alt: Reference, positive and negative series feeding one encoder trained with a triplet loss
body.caption: TRILITE's setup: reference, positive and negative series pass through one encoder trained with a triplet loss. Figure from the TRILITE code repository.

body: My main experiment was multivariate time series classification (MTSC). Disjoint-CNN handles multivariate data by separating temporal and spatial (channel-wise) convolutions. I built a custom variant and ran it next to the original, then plotted the training accuracy and results of both to see where the changes helped and where they didn't.

The scatter plot below puts each dataset at (custom accuracy, original accuracy). Points under the diagonal are datasets where my version did better: 15 for the custom model, 5 for the original and 1 tie.

body.alt: One-to-one accuracy comparison between custom and original Disjoint-CNN
body.caption: Custom vs. original Disjoint-CNN, one point per dataset.

list: Write scripts, not notebooks, for anything you will run more than twice.
Save every result with its configuration, or you will not know what produced it.
A negative result is still a result. Plot it and move on.
Read the evaluation section first: it tells you what the authors were really optimising.

body: I kept working on the Disjoint-CNN code after the internship, with the last updates in August 2024.

title: Starting at AgileSolutions: CRMs, Dialers and RabbitMQ
summary: Back to full-stack work: Node.js and React across many CRM and dialer projects, with social media messages flowing through RabbitMQ.
body: In August 2024 I joined AgileSolutions LLC as a full-stack developer, going back to product work after my research internship. Since then I have worked on around twenty CRM and dialer projects, with Node.js on the backend and React on the frontend.

One of the most interesting parts of the job is handling social media messages. Messages arrive from many channels at unpredictable rates, and losing one is not acceptable. RabbitMQ sits in the middle: producers publish incoming messages and consumers process them at their own pace.

list: Traffic spikes are absorbed by the queue instead of crashing a service.
A consumer can be restarted or deployed without losing messages.
New channels can be added without touching the processing logic.

body.h: Working on many projects at once

body: Twenty projects means you can't afford to solve the same problem twice. That is where a lot of my side projects come from: whenever I notice a pattern repeating, I try to turn it into something reusable.

title: Chess with Tkinter, MSSQL and a Minimax Bot
summary: A desktop chess game in Python with a minimax AI opponent and game data stored in Microsoft SQL Server.
body: Almost two years after my first Tkinter games, I came back to the same toolkit for something much bigger: chess. Comparing the two projects is a good way to see how much I have grown.

list: Tkinter for the desktop UI.
The python-chess library for move generation and rule validation.
Microsoft SQL Server to store game data.
A minimax algorithm for the bot player.

body: Chess rules are full of edge cases: castling, en passant, promotion, stalemate. Using a library for move validation let me focus on what was actually interesting, the AI.

The bot looks a few moves ahead. It assumes it will pick the best move for itself and that I will pick the move that is worst for it, then scores the resulting positions. Even a shallow search with simple material scoring plays a surprisingly annoying game.
I have kept improving the project since then, most recently in June 2026.

title: One Filter Format, Four ORMs
summary: dynamic-query-builder turns flat filters like price_gte=10 into Prisma, Mongoose, TypeORM or Sequelize queries.
body: Across many CRM projects I kept writing the same code: read filters from the query string and turn them into a database query. The only thing that changed was the ORM. So I wrote dynamic-query-builder.
Filters come in as a flat object where each key is field_condition and each value is the value to compare against:
The library has one builder per ORM: buildPrismaQuery, buildMongooseQuery, buildTypeORMQuery and buildSequelizeQuery. For Sequelize you pass in its Op object as well.

list: lt, lte, gt, gte: comparisons.
between: a range, given as an array of two values.
contains (alias c): case-insensitive match; caseSensitiveContains (alias csc).
eq, ne, and the default (no suffix) for equality.
neContains: does not contain.

body: Flat keys survive URLs, forms and logs without any extra encoding, and the frontend doesn't need to know which database is behind the API. The backend can switch from Mongoose to Prisma without changing a single request.

title: A Fully Local Voice AI Assistant in Azerbaijani
summary: Speak into the mic, get a spoken answer: Whisper for speech-to-text, Ollama for the LLM, Edge TTS for the voice, plus a knowledge base.
body: Most voice assistants are built for English. I wanted one that understands Azerbaijani, answers from my own knowledge base, and runs entirely on my own machine. The result is AI Səs Konfransı, a voice-based assistant you can talk to in the browser.

list: Speech-to-text: Whisper large-v3 transcribes the microphone input.
Retrieval: a sentence-transformer model finds relevant entries in the knowledge base.
LLM: a model served by Ollama (for example llama3) writes the answer.
Text-to-speech: Edge TTS reads the answer back.

body: A FastAPI app served with uvicorn ties it all together, and the UI is a simple page with a microphone button.

The target was modest hardware: an NVIDIA RTX 3050 with 4 GB of VRAM. Whisper large-v3 is about 1.5 GB and the embedding model about 120 MB, both downloaded on first launch. The trick is to keep the models loaded between requests and let Ollama run as a separate service.
No API keys, no per-request costs, and no audio leaving the machine. For a knowledge base that may contain internal documents, that last point matters most.
A day later I started whisper-bot, a Telegram bot built on the same speech-to-text idea.

title: Splitting a CRM into Micro-Frontends with Vite
summary: A shell app and three remotes (Customers, Deals, Dashboard) wired together at runtime with Module Federation for Vite.
body: After working on many CRMs, I wanted to try a different architecture: what if each business domain were its own app, built and deployed independently? crm-microfrontend is a small experiment that does exactly that, using Vite, React and @originjs/vite-plugin-federation.

body.code:
shell/      host app (5000): layout, routing, auth, profile, settings
customers/  remote (5001): exposes CustomersApp
deals/      remote (5002): exposes DealsApp
dashboard/  remote (5003): exposes DashboardApp

body: The shell loads the remotes at runtime. Business pages (Customers, Deals, Dashboard) are remotes. Cross-cutting concerns (auth, layout, profile, settings, notifications) stay in the shell, because they apply to every page instead of belonging to one domain.

Each app keeps its own mock data and its own small stylesheet with shared design tokens. Copying those tokens feels wrong at first, but it is the point: a team can change and ship the Deals app without coordinating a release of a shared package.

Micro-frontends add real complexity. They pay off when several teams own different parts of a large product. For a single team, a well-structured monolith is usually simpler. The experiment helped me understand where that line is.

title: World Energy and Temperature Statistics with awk and gnuplot
summary: A team research project: cleaning per-country energy and temperature data with awk, joining it, and turning it into charts with gnuplot.

cover.alt: Top 5 coal, oil and gas producers in 1990 and 2013

body: In September 2022 I worked with two teammates, Azad Kichibekov and Emil Aliyev, on a data analysis project. The question was simple: how have energy production, energy consumption and temperature changed across countries since 1990? We answered it with command-line tools: awk to process the data and gnuplot to draw it.

list: Energy: 241 CSV files, one per country or region, with production and consumption figures for coal, oil, gas, hydro, solar, wind and more.
Temperature: the GlobalLandTemperaturesByCountry dataset, with monthly average temperatures and their uncertainty for every country.

body: Most of the work was getting two very different datasets into one shape. We wrote a small awk script for each step and kept them in a com/ folder so they could be chained:

list: Merge the 241 energy files into one CSV, keeping only the first header.
Keep only the years from 1990 onwards.
Turn monthly dates (yyyy-mm-dd) into years.
Drop rows with missing temperature or uncertainty values.
Group by year and country and average the monthly temperatures.
Join the temperature and energy data on year and country.

body: This is the step that turns monthly dates into years:
I worked on the visualization side. Every chart is a gnuplot script fed by a one-line awk filter, run from a Jupyter notebook, so any chart can be rebuilt from the raw data with a single command.

body.alt: Top 5 coal, oil and gas producers in 1990 compared to 2013
body.caption: Top 5 producers of coal, oil and gas in 1990 (top row) and 2013 (bottom row).

body: Comparing 1990 with 2013 showed the biggest shifts. In 1990 China, the United States and Europe were close in coal production. By 2013 China's coal production was several times higher than anyone else's. In gas, Russia led in 1990, while the United States had moved to first place by 2013.

body.alt: Top 5 hydro, solar and wind consumers in 2013
body.caption: Top 5 consumers of hydro, solar and wind energy in 2013.

body: For renewables in 2013, China led in hydro, while Europe led in both solar and wind, with Germany as the top single country for solar.

body.alt: Greenhouse gas emissions in Azerbaijan from 2000 to 2013, and the top 5 emitters in 2013
body.caption: Left: greenhouse gas emissions in Azerbaijan, 2000 to 2013. Right: the top 5 emitters in 2013.

body: I also plotted average temperatures for France, Germany, Europe, Turkey and Azerbaijan in 1990, 1995, 2000 and 2010. Turkey and Azerbaijan were both about two degrees warmer in 2010 than in 1990.

body.alt: Average temperatures of five countries in 1990, 1995, 2000 and 2010
body.caption: Average temperature in five countries across four years.

list: awk is still one of the fastest ways to filter, group and join CSV files, and a pipeline of small scripts is easy to debug.
Datasets mix countries with regions like "Europe" and "Africa". You have to decide on purpose whether to compare them, or the top 5 charts will mislead you.
Missing values are everywhere. Deciding how to handle them, before averaging anything, mattered more than any chart setting.
Keeping every chart as a script made it painless to fix a mistake and rebuild every chart in minutes.

body: It was my first research-style project, long before my internship at IRIMAS, and it taught me to spend most of my time understanding and cleaning the data.

title: My First Mobile App: A Social Network in Flutter
summary: Posts, comments, follows and a personal feed, built with Flutter and Firebase, with Cloud Functions doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes.
body: My first mobile app was an ambitious one: a small social network. I built it with Flutter and Firebase and pushed it to GitHub between 18 and 20 October 2022.

list: Sign up, log in (including Google sign-in), and reset a forgotten password with Firebase Auth.
Upload posts with images or videos, stored in Firebase Storage.
Comment on posts, follow people and search for users.
See a personal feed (I called it the "flow") of posts from the people you follow.
Edit your profile and read announcements.

body.h: The interesting part: building the feed

body: The hardest question was how to show each user a feed of posts from everyone they follow. Querying every followed account on each app launch would be slow. Instead I used Firebase Cloud Functions to copy posts into a separate feed collection for each follower, as soon as something changes:

list: When you follow someone, their existing posts are copied into your feed.
When you unfollow them, their posts are removed from your feed.
When someone publishes, edits or deletes a post, the change is pushed to all of their followers' feeds.

body: This pattern is called fan-out on write. It makes writes a bit more expensive, but reading a feed becomes a single, fast query. I didn't know the name at the time, but it is how many real social apps work.

Flutter showed me that one codebase can produce a real mobile app, and Firebase showed me that a backend can be just a set of rules and triggers. Two days later I started my next Flutter app, a vocabulary app.

title: A Vocabulary App with 175,000 Phrases, Offline
summary: My second Flutter app: search a French–English phrase list offline and build your own vocabulary in Azerbaijani, English, Turkish and Russian.
body: Right after my first Flutter app, I built something I wanted to use myself: a vocabulary app for learning French. I wrote it on 22 and 23 October 2022.

body.alt: Four screens of the vocabulary app: search, a saved word, the phrase list and the add word form
body.caption: Searching phrases, a saved word with its translations, the full phrase list, and the form to add a new word.

list: French–English: a built-in list of 175,622 phrase pairs. You type a word and see every phrase that uses it, such as "cours" in "Je cours tous les jours".
Your Vocabulary: words you add yourself, with a French word and its translation in Azerbaijani, Russian, English and Turkish.

body: A phrase list that big has to work without a network connection, and it has to search fast. The app ships the phrases as JSON and stores everything in a local SQLite database through the sqflite package. Searching, adding and deleting words all happen on the device, with no backend at all.

After a Firebase app, this was the opposite approach: everything local. It taught me to choose the storage based on the data. Shared, social data belongs in the cloud. Large, read-only reference data and personal notes work better on the phone.
In December 2023 I added screenshots to the README, and in March 2024 I set up Dependabot to keep its packages up to date.

title: My First Data Science Tools: Streamlit and Web Scraping
summary: A three-page Streamlit app for exploring and modelling a dataset, and scrapers built with BeautifulSoup and Scrapy.
body: In September 2022, around the end of my time as a Python mentor at DataScience Academy, I wrote two small projects that taught me the basics of working with data: a Streamlit app and a few web scrapers.

body.h: A machine learning app in three pages

body: The Streamlit app turns a dataset into an interactive tool. A sidebar switches between three pages:

list: Home: a description of the dataframe and its columns.
EDA: null value checks, imputation choices for categorical and numeric columns, imbalance checks, and plots (KDE, box, violin, swarm and bar).

Modelling: pick a scaler (Standard, MinMax or Robust), encode the data, split it, train models such as logistic regression, a decision tree or Gaussian Naive Bayes, and read the classification report.

body: Making every step a dropdown taught me something important: each preprocessing choice changes the result, and seeing it change live is the fastest way to understand why.

The next day I published my scraping notebooks. With requests and BeautifulSoup I collected listing locations and links from bina.az, a real estate site in Azerbaijan, and post titles and votes from a Reddit community. I also tried Scrapy on its practice site, quotes.toscrape.com.
Most data science work happens before the model: getting the data, cleaning it, and understanding it. These two projects were my first real practice at that.

title: Finbiz: My Code Academy Final Project
summary: A responsive business website built in two weeks with Sass, vanilla JavaScript, a small Express API and Jest tests. My teacher liked it a lot.
body: Finbiz was my final frontend project at Code Academy. I built it between 10 and 22 July 2023, in about 50 commits, and I was proud when my teacher really liked the result.

body.alt: Finbiz home page with the headline Let's create your success
body.caption: The Finbiz home page, still live on Vercel.

body: The commit history reads like a diary. I built the home page section by section (header, banner, business progress, about, slideshow, team, testimonials), then the contact and blog pages, and then spent a whole day making every section responsive. Each step went through a develop branch and a pull request.

list: Sass split into abstracts (variables, mixins, animations), base, components, layout and pages, compiled into one compressed CSS file.
Vanilla JavaScript for the slideshow, tabs, a video modal and the blog page.
A small Express server that serves the team, services, latest posts and blog data.
Blog pagination and search, plus a details page for each post.
Jest tests with jsdom that load the HTML and check its structure and styles.

body: The task was a frontend project, but I wanted the pages to load real data instead of hard-coded HTML. Adding the Express API and loading states made the site feel like a real product, and writing tests for HTML and CSS was something new for me.
The project is still maintained: Dependabot keeps its dependencies updated, most recently in September 2026.

title: Learning Computer Graphics with OpenGL and Python
summary: From drawing circles and moving cubes to a small 3D scene with a moving camera, lighting and a day/night cycle.
body: At the end of 2023 I learned computer graphics with OpenGL in Python. After years of building UIs out of HTML elements, drawing every shape myself was a very different experience.

In November 2023 I published my lab work: drawing circles, placing a cone on a circle, and animating moving cubes. These exercises are all about transformations. You translate, rotate and scale a shape, and the order of those operations completely changes the result.

body.h: A scene with a day/night cycle

body: In December 2023 I put it together in a small 3D scene with PyOpenGL and GLUT:

list: A camera you can move around, with yaw and pitch for looking around.
A light source with ambient and diffuse lighting.
A day/night toggle on a timer that changes the sky colour and the brightness of the whole scene.

body: Graphics programming made matrices and vectors concrete. A camera is just a transformation, and lighting is just maths on surface normals. It also gave me a lot of respect for game engines, which do all of this for you.

title: Logistic Regression from Scratch vs. Deep Learning
summary: I wrote a multi-class logistic regression in NumPy and compared it with published deep learning results on the UCR archive. It lost, and that was the point.

cover.alt: My logistic regression compared with FCN and MLP

body: At the start of my internship at IRIMAS I wanted a baseline I fully understood before touching deep learning. So I wrote logistic regression from scratch in NumPy and tested it on time series datasets from the UCR archive.

list: One-vs-rest: one binary classifier per class, and the class with the highest score wins.
Sigmoid activation and gradient descent on the weights and a bias.
Mini-batches of 16, a learning rate of 0.01 and 5,000 iterations.

body: I compared my test accuracy with published results for deep learning models on the same datasets: MLP, FCN, ResNet, Encoder, MCNN, MCDCNN, Time-CNN, t-LeNet and TWIESN.

body.alt: Scatter plots comparing logistic regression with FCN and MLP
body.caption: One point per dataset. FCN beat my logistic regression on 14 datasets out of 15, and MLP on 13.

body: The plots show exactly what deep models add on time series. A linear model treats each time step as an unrelated feature, while convolutions find shapes wherever they appear in the series. After this I moved on to MLP, FCN and ResNet, and finally understood why they are built the way they are.

title: Re-implementing FCN, ResNet, ROCKET, InceptionTime and LITE
summary: Two weeks of rebuilding the classic time series classifiers myself, from a 268-minute FCN run to a custom LITE model.

cover.alt: InceptionTime training curves on the Car dataset

body: In February 2024 I set myself a rule: for every important time series classifier, write my own version and get results on the UCR datasets. Each model got its own repository.

I started with an MLP, first without and then with dropout, and then implemented FCN and ResNet. GPUs were my first problem. One commit message from 19 February says it all: "GET RESULTS OF FCN AFTER 268 MINUTES".

ROCKET takes a completely different approach. It generates thousands of random convolution kernels, extracts two simple features from each, and trains a linear RidgeClassifierCV on top. The kernels themselves are never trained.

body.alt: ROCKET train and test accuracy over ten runs on the Car dataset
body.caption: My ROCKET on the Car dataset over 10 runs: perfect training accuracy (blue) and around 88–90% test accuracy (orange).

body: For InceptionTime I trained versions with one, two and three Inception modules to see how depth affects learning, and saved the loss and accuracy curves for each run.

body.alt: InceptionTime loss and accuracy over epochs on the Car dataset
body.caption: Loss and accuracy over epochs on the Car dataset for one of my InceptionTime runs.

body: The last one was LITE, a light Inception-style model. I built a custom LITE model and finished testing it on 28 February 2024.

list: Reading the code of a paper is not the same as understanding it. Writing it is.
Results vary between runs, so always run several times before comparing.
A simple model with random features (ROCKET) can compete with a deep network, and train much faster.

title: Do Two CNNs Learn the Same Filters?
summary: I trained one FCN on the train split and one on the test split of 20 datasets, then compared their first-layer filters with DTW and t-SNE.

cover.alt: t-SNE map of first-layer FCN filters on the Beef dataset

body: Deep learning models are often called black boxes. During my internship I wanted to look inside one, so I asked a simple question: if two FCNs learn from different data drawn from the same problem, do they learn the same filters?

list: For each of 20 UCR datasets, train one FCN on the training split and another on the test split.
Take the 128 filters of the first convolution layer from each model.
Compare the filters using dynamic time warping (DTW) distances, which suit shapes that may be shifted in time.
Project them into 2D with t-SNE, using perplexities of 3, 5, 10 and 15.

body.alt: Scatter plot of first-layer filters from two FCNs on the Beef dataset
body.caption: First-layer filters on the Beef dataset. Blue: the model trained on the train split. Orange: the model trained on the test split.

body: On many datasets the two colours are mixed together: both models end up with filters of similar shapes, even though they never saw the same examples. It suggests that the first layer learns general building blocks of the signal, not details of particular samples.
Trying several perplexities mattered. t-SNE pictures can change a lot with this setting, so a pattern only counts if it shows up in all of them.

title: Classic Machine Learning: Credit Cards and Chemistry
summary: Two team projects with scikit-learn: predicting good and bad credit card clients, and filling gaps in a chemical dataset before classifying molecules.

cover.alt: Pie chart of surfactant head families

body: On 23 February 2024 I published several machine learning notebooks from team projects, together with a ridge and lasso regression study. Two of them taught me the most.

The task was to decide whether an applicant is a "good" or "bad" client. The catch: the dataset doesn't say what "bad" means, so the label has to be built from the repayment history, for example with a vintage analysis.
The second catch was imbalance. Almost every client was "good", so a model that always says "good" looks accurate and is useless.

body.alt: Class balance before and after oversampling
body.caption: Target classes before balancing (99.6% to 0.4%) and after oversampling (50/50).

body: After cleaning and feature engineering, we compared K-means, SVC and logistic regression, using pipelines and GridSearchCV for hyperparameters, before and after fixing the imbalance.

The second project used a dataset of 199 surfactant molecules with 18 attributes, collected from scientific papers. Many values were missing, and instead of just using the mean, we filled several of them with chemistry formulas: molar mass, Amin and the critical micelle concentration (CMC).

body.alt: Pie chart of head families in the dataset
body.caption: The head families we tried to predict from CMC, surface tension and Amin.

body: After encoding, robust scaling and oversampling, we compared four classifiers. With GridSearchCV the decision tree reached 91.8%, random forest 91.6%, KNN 90.7% and SVC 85.1%.
In both projects the model was the easy part. Defining the label, handling imbalance and filling missing values correctly made the real difference.

title: Building an Online UNO Game in React Native
summary: A card game app with Firebase sign-in, chat and tournaments, which I took online with real-time multiplayer and +4 bluff challenges.
body: UNO is my longest-running mobile project. I started it in August 2024, and on 28 December 2025 I made the biggest change: real online multiplayer.

body.h: From Expo to React Native CLI

body: My first React Native code was two small Expo apps, a cars catalogue and a book list with a details screen, which I uploaded in May 2023. For UNO I needed native Firebase modules and Google sign-in, so on day one I moved from Expo to the React Native CLI.

list: Firebase Auth with Google sign-in.
A users screen, chat rooms and tournaments.
An offline game, with all the game rules in a React context.

body: Online play meant the game state could no longer live on one phone. I added an online cards context that syncs the deck, players' hands and turns through Firebase, while the same UI components work for both offline and online games.

list: Turn management that stays correct when several players act.
+2 and +4 cards that give the penalty to the right player and move the turn correctly.
A bluff challenge: when someone plays a +4, the next player can challenge it as a bluff.
Choosing a colour after a wild card, synced to everyone.
Fewer re-renders in the game and chat screens, by keeping previous values in refs.

body: In March 2026 I added a mode for more players.
A card game looks simple until several phones have to agree on the same state. Most of the work was making sure every action produced exactly one correct state change, no matter who acted first.
